articles.title: AI Shopping Bots Buy The Wrong Thing, WeFetch Says Barcodes Fix It
articles.description: WeFetch AI Corp., formerly GreenCore Solutions Corp., has completed its name change as it pitches a barcode check that stops AI shopping agents from buying the wrong product. Key Takeaways The Registrar of Companies for British Columbia issued the Certificate of Change of Name on Nov. 13, 2026 The lead product, gtinfetch.ai, answers for 84,810,515 barcodes from 376,271 makers across 3,520,471 points of sale Each check gets a signed receipt at rco.wefetch.ai that is open to public verification The full record now answers from France, Singapore and the United States The company announced that it has completed its change of name. It describes itself as an artificial intelligence (AI) shopping company. Its lead product, gtinfetch.ai, is built to remove the guesswork when an AI agent picks a product. How The Barcode Check Works The company says an AI agent picks a product in words, and the same words can match a dozen barcodes. Examples include the right brand in the wrong size, last year's pack, or a look-alike from another maker. When the agent guesses, the company says the shopper gets the wrong product, the brand loses a sale it had already won, and the retailer pays for the return. With gtinfetch.ai, an AI agent sends a barcode and gets a firm answer: verified, not verified or unknown, with the sources behind it. Signed Receipts And Three Regions The company says that when an AI agent buys for a shopper, the agent's choice leaves no record today. gtinfetch.ai gives the agent a signed receipt of the check, written at rco.wefetch.ai and open to public verification. Retailers, brands and auditors can see what was checked, when, and what the answer was. The mark is "Barcode verified". The full record now answers from France, Singapore and the United States. Every barcode also has its own free public page at gtinfetch.ai. The company says these three regions are where AI shopping starts. It cited figures from a Microsoft AI Diffusion Report for the second quarter of 2026 on consumer use of generative AI among working-age people. Region Working-age people using generative AI Singapore 64.3% France 49.6% United States 33.0% Worldwide 18.8% The company also calls them the home markets of the AI that shoppers ask. It names ChatGPT and Claude in the United States and Mistral in France. What The Company Says It Built The company describes WeFetch.ai as a barcode fetch system for AI agents. It says the system answers for 84 million products in 70 countries, with 3.5 million points of sale on its own record. Every answer is signed. The product set includes triggerfetch for brands, shopfetch for shoppers, matchfetch for AI agents and gtinfetch as the record itself. The company says it works with ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Grok, Mistral, Perplexity and Muse. "Words were the first generation of AI answers. Barcodes are agentic commerce," said Matthew Keddy, Chief Executive Officer of WeFetch AI Corp. The company also cited a Gartner forecast of $2.7 trillion in AI spending in 2026. It cited a McKinsey projection that AI agents will orchestrate $3 trillion to $5 trillion in global commerce by 2030, up to $1 trillion of it in US retail. articles.title: OpenStack Horizon's exact-name zero hides the dashboard path
articles.description: OpenStack Horizon's exact-name zero hides the dashboard path OpenStack Horizon is the canonical dashboard for OpenStack. It gives tenants a web interface for provisioning and managing resources and gives administrators a management view. The browser may identify the service as "OpenStack Dashboard," a tenant name, a branded portal, or a generic login page. An exact search for "OpenStack Horizon" can therefore be less useful than the deployment path and identity flow. The 2026-11-16 count-only observation used sub_type=all, page 1, and pagesize 1. app="OpenStack Horizon" returned 0, title="OpenStack Horizon" returned 0, and http.body="OpenStack Horizon" returned 96. Those counts do not measure the number of OpenStack clouds. Query role Exact dork Observed total Application fingerprint app="OpenStack Horizon" 0 Page title title="OpenStack Horizon" HTTP body http.body="OpenStack Horizon" 96 The dashboard is an identity and authorization surface OpenStack's security guide describes the dashboard as a self-service portal backed by the Identity service. Horizon itself is a Django application, and its deployment inherits Django security practices such as allowed hosts, secure cookies, CSRF protection, and authentication configuration. The important inventory fields are the dashboard URL, Keystone endpoint, federation or local authentication method, allowed hosts, session backend, and administrator paths. A login page does not show which OpenStack services the tenant can reach or whether an administrator view is disabled. Product branding varies Horizon can be customized with site branding and deployed under a path such as /horizon/. A dashboard behind a proxy may return a generic login title. A documentation site may contain the full name without running Horizon. The 96 body results are a lead set for checking URLs, headers, login forms, and paths. The zero exact-name observations show the weakness of those two labels, not the absence of Horizon deployments. Search planning should include configuration terms, static asset paths, and the expected authentication redirects, but every query must still be validated. Separate tenant and administrator decisions Tenant actions such as creating instances or changing security groups are sensitive. Administrator actions can alter quotas, users, networks, or service configuration. A dashboard should not assume that the login page protects both planes equally. Role checks belong in the backend services as well as Horizon. Review whether federation metadata is current, whether session cookies are marked secure and HTTP-only, whether the application trusts proxy headers, and whether error pages reveal service endpoints. Test with designated accounts and a defined scope. Use the selected body observation as a route clue The body query is the only nonzero selected observation and supplies the link below. It should be treated as a candidate-discovery step. An organization can correlate those candidates with its own Keystone endpoints and dashboard hostnames, then validate the actual response. The operational lesson is that an OpenStack dashboard is identified by its role in a cloud control plane, not by a two-word title match. A zero on the exact name can coexist with a well-used dashboard. Asset records should follow the identity provider, the dashboard URL, and the services it can reach. References OpenStack Dashboard security guide OpenStack management interfaces Horizon login documentation ZoomEye count-only observation

articles.title: Italy Fines Meta €805M For Opening 20M Facebook Users' Photo Galleries
articles.description: Italy's privacy regulator fined Meta €805 million after the Facebook app on Android phones reached into about 20 million Italian users' photo galleries without their specific consent. Key Takeaways The fine of €805 million is about 0.47% of Meta's worldwide group turnover About 20 million Android users in Italy were affected by a gallery suggestions feature running since 2023 Meta has 60 days to ask for separate consent and switch the feature off by default The regulator said Meta cooperated poorly during the investigation The Garante per la protezione dei dati personali announced the penalty on Nov. 14 against Meta Platforms Ireland Limited. The case covers a Facebook feature that suggests photos and videos from a user's phone gallery as post ideas while they scroll. How Facebook Got Into The Gallery According to the regulator, Facebook asked for gallery access through one permission that covered the whole app and several features with different purposes. That request came after a vague prompt to "enable other features", which never made clear that gallery suggestions were part of it. The feature was switched on by default. Once users granted full access, the app could read their entire photo library, generally for good. The regulator said neither users nor the authority itself could check what data was actually used. The investigation began in July 2025 after a complaint from a consumer group in Bolzano, and the authority ran its own technical tests on the app. Why Italy Acted Instead Of Ireland Meta argued that Ireland's data regulator should handle the case, since Meta's European arm is based there. The Italian authority rejected that. It acted under the Italian rule that puts a phone's contents inside a person's private sphere, which comes from the EU's ePrivacy law, and that law has no single lead regulator for companies operating across the bloc. Under that rule, any access to what is stored on a phone needs free and informed consent, whether or not the data leaves the device or anyone is harmed. What Meta Must Do Deadline Report the steps it has started 30 days Ask for separate, specific consent for gallery suggestions and keep the feature off by default 60 days Report the measures it has adopted 90 days What Made The Fine Bigger The regulator cited the number of people affected, the fact that the breach is still running for users who have not updated the app or already gave permission, an earlier 2019 measure against Meta and Meta's poor cooperation. It gave some credit for changes Meta made after the complaint but called them late, since they only reach users who update the app. If Meta misses the 60-day deadline, the feature cannot be switched on for anyone who has not given valid consent. The AI Question Left Open The case did not look at whether gallery photos are used to train AI, and Meta denies doing so. The regulator said it may separately examine a new feature launched in 2026 that processes gallery content in the cloud. articles.title: Card testing hides inside your own decline rate
articles.description: We found card testing on a checkout by accident. A merchant's approval rate fell from 81% to 64% in two days. The first guess was an issuer problem or a routing bug. It was neither. The logs showed about 3,000 attempts an hour from a few hundred IPs. Each attempt was a $1 authorization with a different PAN, and almost all were declined. A few percent were approved, and that was the point: the attacker was checking which stolen cards were still live. The checkout endpoint had no limit on failed attempts per session, per IP, or per BIN range. It accepted anonymous POSTs and returned a clean decline code each time. We had effectively built a card validity oracle and handed it out for free. The fix was boring: Cap failed attempts per session and per device fingerprint, not just per IP. Botnets rotate IPs. Add a CAPTCHA or 3DS step after the second decline. Return the same generic message for every decline reason on the client side. Keep the real code in your logs. Alert on decline ratio per hour, not per day. A daily average hides a four-hour burst. The scheme-side cost matters too. Acquirers and card networks watch your decline ratio and can flag you for it, even if every card was stolen by someone else. Where do you put the first rate limit: at the edge, in the app, or at the gateway? Which layer has worked for you? Cache Repeated Answers to Cut LLM Calls in a Small-Business FAQ Bot (Python + SQLite)
articles.description: Small businesses get the same ten questions all day: opening hours, delivery areas, how to book. Sending each one to a language model is wasted money. A small cache is one of the simplest ways to control AI automation costs for a small business. Normalise, then hash import hashlib, re, sqlite3, time db = sqlite3.connect("answers.db") db.execute("""CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS cache( key TEXT PRIMARY KEY, question TEXT, answer TEXT, created REAL, hits INTEGER DEFAULT 0)""") def normalise(q: str) -> str: q = q.lower() q = re.sub(r"[^a-z0-9 ]+", " ", q) return " ".join(q.split()) def key(q: str) -> str: return hashlib.sha256(normalise(q).encode()).hexdigest() Read through the cache MAX_AGE = 7 * 24 * 3600 # refresh weekly so answers do not go stale def answer(q, call_model): k = key(q) row = db.execute("SELECT answer, created FROM cache WHERE key=?", (k,)).fetchone() if row and time.time() - row[1] < MAX_AGE: return row[0], "cache" a = call_model(q) return a, "model" Rules that keep it safe Cache only general questions. Never cache answers that include a customer's name, order or account details. Expire entries when prices, hours or policies change (clear the table on any website update). Log cache versus model so you can see what the cache actually saves. Going further Exact matching catches more than you expect once text is normalised. Fuzzy or embedding matching adds complexity; measure first. Why we often prefer small custom pieces like this over packaged bots: why small custom pieces often beat packaged bots. Disclosure: I co-founded NxFlowAI, an automation agency.

articles.title: Observal AI coding agent observability: sessions and traces
articles.description: A developer tells you: « the agent ran for an hour, burned a pile of tokens and shipped nothing. » There is no error code and no stack trace, only a conversation. For that case, Observal AI coding agent observability means keeping the session itself, which is the ground Observal covers: an open source repository (Apache 2.0) showing about 4.3k stars on the GitHub page I read on 9 November 2026. This post approaches it through the operational decision it forces on you: what to keep from an agent session, where, and for whom. A note on method: span.observer did not deploy Observal. Everything below comes from the README, the repository documentation and the screenshots it publishes; anything I could not read is marked « unverified ». Observal AI coding agent observability: what is it? First trap: the name moved. The README now calls itself « Agentic Resource Registry » and states « Formerly Observal: same code, same maintainers, same Apache 2.0 license ». The command is still observal and old links redirect. Today the project describes itself as a self-hosted registry of resources for coding agents (skills, MCP servers, hooks, prompts, sandboxes) with a session-tracing layer on top. If you were looking for an LLM benchmark-style evaluation platform, that is not what the documentation describes (see limits below). Facts taken from the repository: Apache 2.0 licence, Python on the server and CLI (FastAPI, Typer), React for the UI, PostgreSQL 16 for the registry, ClickHouse for telemetry, Redis for the queue. The latest commit on the main branch is dated 7 November 2026 and pyproject.toml carries version 1.17.0-dev.0; I could not read a published release on the page, so I quote no stable number. The fork count (about 1.1k) comes from the same page. What it records from an agent session The mechanism is easy to state. A hook or extension in the harness (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Copilot, Kiro, OpenCode, Pi, Goose, Antigravity according to the README) reads the conversation transcript and sends it to the server. The CLI first writes to a durable local outbox, then posts to /api/v1/ingest/session; the server returns the highest acknowledged position, and delivery is described as « at-least-once with effectively-once storage ». observal reconcile replays what is missing from the local source. Each record becomes an event: prompt, response, tool call, result, token update, error, subagent. Per-session aggregates (tokens, models, tools, duration) feed the dashboards. The documentation is frank about a useful limit: detail depends on what the harness writes, and Observal does not intercept MCP traffic or invent fields. Interface tour: sessions, turns, calls The next screenshot comes from the repository (docs/img, covered by the project’s Apache 2.0 licence). It shows a Pi session: duration, 17 turns, input and output tokens, cache reads, tool call count, models, then the expandable list of turns with their duration. The session list gives the overview: platform, input and output tokens, tools called, duration, and a « Score » column that stays empty in this demo capture. It is the only evaluation hint I read there; I do not know when or how that score is filled. From complaint to diagnosis: the documented method The « Debug agent failures » guide walks through four moves, which I paraphrase: find the session (filters by harness, agent, model, period), read the events in order, inspect tool call detail, then patch delivery gaps with observal reconcile. Its pattern table is the most telling part: the same tool re-called with identical arguments points to a loop; a call with no result suggests an abrupt stop or an incomplete transcript; an expected MCP call that never shows up means the model did not pick it, or the harness did not record it. The commands in the capture below are those of the README and that guide. Installing Observal: server first, CLI second Per the README there are two parts: a server to host (API, web UI, databases) and a CLI on each workstation. The server needs Docker Engine 24 or later with Compose v2; the install-server.sh script downloads a Compose package, generates secret files, binds ports to loopback by default and starts ten services. For the CLI: an install.sh script (macOS, Linux), install.ps1 (Windows) or uv tool install observal-cli on Python 3.11 or later. Then: observal auth login observal doctor --patch The second command detects the harness and installs the telemetry hooks. An operator’s tip: these installs go through curl | bash. Download the script, read it, and try it on a throwaway machine before pointing real sessions at it. I did not run these commands. Observing Observal itself The project applies observability to its own stack, without OpenTelemetry. According to its self-observability page: /livez and /readyz probes (the latter checks PostgreSQL, ClickHouse and Redis), JSON logs with a request ID carried by the X-Request-ID header, and Prometheus metrics on /metrics (request counter, latency histogram, memory, CPU). A Prometheus and a Grafana ship in the Compose file. On the agent side, the Claude Code integration page tells you not to set the OTEL_* variables or CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_TELEMETRY: Observal does not consume OTLP telemetry and relies only on its hooks and reconciliation. If you want OpenTelemetry metrics on your agents, that is a different pipeline; see monitoring coding agents in the enterprise. The project documents no Dynatrace integration, and we assume none. Limits and open points Evaluation: I found no benchmark or quality test set. There are LLM-generated « Insights » reports (through LiteLLM, with the provider you choose) summarising what helps or hinders, which is usage analysis, not a correctness measure. Privacy: a session contains your prompts, command output and sometimes paths or secrets. Decide on retention (the databases page mentions retention policies) and on who may read what before deploying. Maturity: a development version, a changelog with a busy « Unreleased » section, and the Leaderboard is announced there as off by default. Expect movement. Coverage: detail varies by harness; a poor transcript gives a poor trace. Weight: ten services to watch agents is a real infrastructure project. Good practices Start with one harness and one pilot team, on an isolated server. Keep ports on loopback or behind an authenticated proxy, as the default does. Monitor the stack with /readyz and Prometheus; learn to repair gaps with observal reconcile. Pair session traces with cost tracking: see AI agent cost from OpenTelemetry token metrics. Put guardrails upstream, as in AI agent guardrails in production. For a neighbouring repository, read kagent, AI agents on Kubernetes. Frequently asked questions Is Observal still the project’s name? The README presents it as Agentic Resource Registry, « formerly Observal », with the same code base and licence; the CLI is still called observal. Does Observal evaluate the quality of an agent’s answers? I did not read any automatic evaluation feature: the project records sessions and produces usage reports. A score column exists in the UI, with no explanation I could verify. Do I need OpenTelemetry to use it? No: ingestion goes through hooks and reconciliation, and the documentation advises against enabling Claude Code’s OTLP telemetry for this integration. Conclusion Observal answers a concrete question: what happened in that agent session? Its strength is the kept, replayable trace; its limits are a heavy stack, little visible evaluation and a project still on the move. For a team that lets agents work on its code, it deserves an isolated trial, with a clear decision about the data it keeps. span.observer is an independent community blog, not affiliated with the Observal project, its maintainers or Dynatrace LLC. Trademarks belong to their owners. Tools change quickly: check commands and options in their official documentation. Originally published on span.observer. articles.title: Write the test plan before your coding agent writes code
articles.description: When a coding agent writes code faster than you can read it, reading every line stops working as review, and approved tests have to carry most of that load. So define the tests before the agent writes any implementation, read them yourself, and require every commit to pass them. Your attention moves from reading diffs to deciding what "done" means. Anush Elangovan is Corporate VP of AI Software at AMD. Before we recorded his April 2026 episode, he told me he was generating 250,000 lines of code a week with AI agents. Lines of code isn't a measure of success, but it shows the throughput problem: no human reviews that volume line by line. By the time we talked, he said a week had earlier come to about 4.2 billion tokens, a check that morning showed 6.5 billion consumed, and he could no longer keep track of lines. Why write tests before the agent writes code? Because the tests are the only fixed point while the implementation churns. Anush held this view before agents existed: Yeah, so my philosophy is, even before agentic coding, I used to advise people and friends and colleagues, 80% of your time should be spent on tests and writing tests. Even before you write your first line of code, you should have a test framework. Anush Elangovan, Corporate VP of AI Software at AMD, on Chain of Thought ep 56 250,000 Lines of Code/Week: In… - Chain of Thought | AI Agents, Infrastructure & Engineering - Apple Podcasts Podcast Episode · Chain of Thought | AI Agents, Infrastructure & Engineering · April 22 · 51m podcasts.apple.com With agents, the tests also do the job a reviewer used to do. When he doesn't like something about the output, he turns it into a stronger gate instead of arguing with the agent: Yep, testing is the code review and testing is kind of the gate of your sandbox. If you have a complaint about anything in the box, fix the sandbox, right? That includes non-functional requirements. For his virtual GPU simulator he set a performance metric, each dispatch executing in 50 microseconds of simulator time. When a change fails that test, the agent has to find another approach. How do you check the tests an agent proposes? Read them before you approve them. Anush's example: an agent wanted to implement GPU demand paging in one go. He stopped it and told it to write 100 tests covering combinations and corner cases first. Some of the tests were repetitive, with parameters changed but not the thing being tested. After reading them, he was satisfied that if the set passed, the feature was good. Things to look for in an agent-written test list: The same assertion with only literal values changed. Missing negative cases, or platforms you named in the plan but no test covers. Mocks that remove the behavior you care about, which make passing cheap. His reason for the scrutiny is that agents optimize for the gate: they try to just reward hack their way towards that test. So all you have to think of is like, they cannot reward hack that, right? Like you're putting up gates that they have to pass through. A minimal sketch to adapt. Test cases are plain records with a content hash, so an agent can't keep an approved test ID while weakening its assertions. def near_duplicates(cases): """cases: list of dicts with 'id', 'target' and 'params' keys.""" seen, dups = {}, [] for c in cases: # same target, same parameter names: probably only values changed key = (c["target"], tuple(sorted(c["params"]))) if key in seen: else: seen[key] = c["id"] return dups def may_implement(proposed, approved): """approved: {test_id: sha256 of the test's source}, frozen at human approval.""" if not approved: return False, "a human has not approved the test list yet" current = {c["id"]: c["sha256"] for c in proposed} changed = [t for t, h in approved.items() if current.get(t) != h] return (not changed), f"approved tests missing or edited: {sorted(changed)}" def commit_passes(approved, current_hashes, ran_ids, failed_ids): # all inputs come from your CI runner, not from the agent's report unchanged = all(current_hashes.get(t) == h for t, h in approved.items()) return bool(approved) and unchanged and set(approved) <= ran_ids and not failed_ids near_duplicates only surfaces candidates for you to read. It won't decide whether two tests cover different behavior. What should gate every commit? The approved suite, plus a test for whatever the commit fixes. Anush rewrote Slurm in Rust as a project called Spur, and he runs an agent that monitors its issue tracker. It picks up filed issues, fixes them, tests and deploys. If CI is green, it ships. His rule is that every commit it makes must include a test for the fix before it's committed. How do you run several agents without losing track? Give each one a job you can describe in a sentence. He doesn't give agents free rein to go off in the weeds or spawn their own thread pools. The Spur agent's job is to wake up at 5 a.m., check for issues, fix what it can and go back to sleep. When it finds an issue it can't fix, he steps in. On the simulator, each ISA transpilation target is its own sub-agent. FAQ Does this mean you never read agent-written code? No. You still read the plan and the tests closely, and you step in when an agent hits an issue it can't fix. What changes is where review effort goes first. Aren't token counts or lines of code a sign the workflow works? No. Both measure throughput. A green run of tests you approved before implementation is the measure that matters. How many tests should you ask for? Enough to cover the corner cases you can name. Anush asked for 100 for demand paging, then read them and found repeats. The count matters less than reading the list. Takeaway Write a short plan, then ask the agent for test cases before any implementation prompt. Read the list, merge near-duplicates, and store the approved IDs where the agent can't change them. Gate every commit on the approved suite passing, and require a test with every fix. Put performance and platform requirements in the suite, not in chat. Give each agent one job, and own what it can't resolve. The full conversation, with the transcript, is on Chain of Thought. Subscribe to the Chain of Thought newsletter for new episodes and write-ups like this one. Drafted with AI assistance from the episode transcripts.

articles.title: Datadog Alternatives: 10 Options and How to Pick One
articles.description: If you are searching for a Datadog alternative, the problem is usually the bill, and a new tool is 1 of 5 ways to fix it: Bottom line There are 5 routes away from your current Datadog bill, and only 4 of them change the tool. Stay and cut the bill: fewer indexed logs, fewer tag combinations, a commitment that fits Another commercial platform: New Relic, Dynatrace, Honeycomb, Elastic Managed open source: Grafana Cloud, SigNoz Cloud Self-hosted open source: Prometheus, Grafana, Loki and Tempo, or SigNoz, or VictoriaMetrics Your cloud's own monitoring: Amazon CloudWatch, Google Cloud Observability The 5 routes away from your Datadog bill. Only 4 of them change the tool. Here is where I would start, by situation: Your situation Start with The bill grew, the tool works Route 1, then compare You are leaving, with under 20 engineers and nobody to run a monitoring stack Grafana Cloud or SigNoz Cloud Data has to stay in your own cloud account Self-hosted Grafana stack or SigNoz You debug requests across many services all day Honeycomb A large company that wants one vendor and one contract Dynatrace or New Relic One cloud, a few services, a small budget CloudWatch or Google Cloud Observability Whatever you pick, the price of the new tool is the smaller cost. The bigger one is moving your instrumentation, your dashboards and your monitors. So do one thing before you pick: send your telemetry through OpenTelemetry. After that, changing the tool is a change of address. All prices here are public list prices in USD, checked on November 15, 2026 against each vendor's pricing page. Your contract can differ. Is the Datadog bill the reason you are reading this? Our senior engineers assess your setup, plan the work and do it hands-on, paid by the hour with no lock-in. Book a free 30-minute consultation. Find your situation: The renewal is close and you need a number: 500 GB of logs and 20,000 metrics, priced on each tool You want to keep Datadog and pay less: Route 1 You want open source and no servers to run: Route 3 You already decided to leave: move to OpenTelemetry first, then run both side by side Know what you use before you compare tools Datadog is a price list of separate products. So is every alternative. Before you open a comparison page, write down which of these you use today: Infrastructure metrics and the integrations that feed them Application tracing (APM) Logs: search, pipelines, archives Dashboards and monitors Synthetic tests and real user monitoring (RUM) On-call and incident tooling Then write down why you want to leave. There are 4 honest reasons: The bill: it grows faster than the system Lock-in: your code and your agents speak one vendor's format Data location: telemetry must stay in your account or your region Fit: you use 2 products out of 20 and pay for a platform Reason = route. A bill problem starts at Route 1. A data location problem starts at Route 4. (A fifth reason exists: someone saw a nicer dashboard at a conference. It is the most expensive one.) Route 1: Cut the Datadog bill and stay This is the cheapest route, and the one that gets skipped. In my Datadog pricing breakdown, a setup of 50 hosts costs $4,360 a month at list price. 3 changes bring it to $2,953: Exclusion filters on the log indexes, so you ingest everything and index a part of it Fewer queryable tags on the custom metrics that multiply APM only on the hosts that send traces you read None of them needs a new tool, a migration or a retrained team. Do this first even if you plan to leave. The filters and the tag cleanup carry over: every tool on this page bills you for volume in some unit. Stay when the bill after the cleanup is one you can defend. Leave when it is still too high, or when the reason was never the bill. Route 2: Another commercial platform These are full platforms run by a vendor. You swap one bill for another, with a different unit. Tool What sets the bill List price Fits New Relic GB ingested, plus full platform users 100 GB a month free, then $0.40 per GB. Full platform users: $10 for the first and $99 for each of the next 4 on Standard (5 at most), $349 each on Pro with an annual commitment Teams that want one product for everything and have few people who need full access Dynatrace Memory of the monitored hosts, per hour, plus GiB ingested Full-Stack Monitoring: $0.01 per memory-GiB-hour ($58 a month for an 8 GiB host). Logs: $0.20 per GiB to ingest Large companies that want automatic instrumentation and an annual contract Events sent Free up to 20 million events a month. Pro starts at $150 a month for 50 million events Teams that debug with traces and wide events, with unlimited seats Elastic Observability GB ingested and GB retained Serverless, Complete tier: ingest "as low as" $0.09 per GB, retention $0.019 per GB a month Teams that already run Elasticsearch and are heavy on logs 3 things to check before you sign: New Relic users: Standard allows 5 full platform users, for $406 a month. From the 6th you are on Pro, where 5 users cost $1,745 a month before 1 GB of data. Basic users are free and can see dashboards. Count who needs more Dynatrace commitment: the pricing page describes a minimum annual spend commitment and prints no amount. Ask for it in the first call Dynatrace host size: a 32 GiB node costs 4 times the 8 GiB price for Full-Stack Monitoring. Check the memory of your nodes before you read the $58 Coralogix and Better Stack also show up on these shortlists. Both price per GB, and both prices depend on the pipeline or the region you choose, so read the full table before you compare. New Relic, Dynatrace, Honeycomb and Elastic all accept OpenTelemetry data over OTLP (the OpenTelemetry Protocol). That matters for the switch, below. Route 3: Managed open source The software is open source. Someone else runs it. You pay for usage, and you can take the same software in-house later. For most startups leaving Datadog, this is the route I would take. Grafana Cloud Grafana Cloud is the hosted version of the Grafana stack: Mimir for metrics, Loki for logs, Tempo for traces, Grafana for dashboards. Free plan: 10,000 active metric series, 50 GB of logs, 50 GB of traces, 14 days of retention, 3 users Pro plan: $19 a month platform fee with the same amounts included, then pay as you go Metrics: from $6.50 per 1,000 active series, kept 13 months Logs and traces: $0.05 per GB to process, $0.40 to write and $0.10 to retain, so $0.55 per GB, kept 30 days Users: from $8 per active Grafana user a month The unit to watch is the active series. Every label value you add creates new series, exactly like tags create custom metrics in Datadog. One more line to plan for: Grafana Cloud's Kubernetes Monitoring app is billed separately, by the host hour ($0.01, about $7.20 a node a month) and the container hour ($0.0007, about $0.50 a container a month), on top of the series and GB it produces. On 50 nodes and 1,000 containers that is about $815 a month. You can skip the app, build your own Kubernetes dashboards and pay for telemetry only. Decide which before you estimate. SigNoz Cloud SigNoz is one application for metrics, traces and logs, built on OpenTelemetry and stored in ClickHouse. Entry: $49 a month, which includes $49 of usage (the pricing page shows $199 struck through next to it, so check it on the day you sign up) Logs and traces: $0.30 per GB, kept 15 days Metrics: $0.10 per million samples, kept 1 month No fee per user or per host SigNoz publishes a guide for migrating from Datadog, and a tool that translates Datadog dashboard JSON into SigNoz dashboards as a starting point. Grafana Cloud = more parts, more integrations, a bigger community. SigNoz = one product, one query screen, a simpler price list. Route 4: Self-hosted open source You run the stack in your own cluster. The licence costs nothing. The work is yours. Stack Licence What you run Prometheus, Grafana, Loki, Tempo (Mimir when 1 Prometheus is too small) Prometheus: Apache 2.0. Grafana, Loki, Tempo and Mimir: AGPLv3 4 or 5 systems, object storage, their upgrades SigNoz community edition MIT, outside its enterprise directories SigNoz and a ClickHouse cluster VictoriaMetrics for metrics, with Grafana on top Apache 2.0 A metrics store that speaks PromQL and also accepts Datadog Agent and DogStatsD metrics What you pay for on this route: Compute, disks and object storage for the telemetry Upgrades of every component Capacity planning when a team adds a label with 10,000 values An on-call rotation for the monitoring itself Self-hosted cost = infrastructure + engineer time. The second number is the big one, and it is missing from every "free alternative" list. My rule: self-host when the managed bill is larger than the engineer time it takes to run the stack, or when the data is not allowed to leave your account. Under about 20 engineers, neither is usually true. I wrote about the stages in how to build a startup observability stack. If you want the open source stack in your own account with someone else operating it, both vendors sell that too, at enterprise prices: Grafana Cloud has a Bring Your Own Cloud option on AWS and GCP (Enterprise starts at $25,000 a year), and SigNoz offers a BYOC plan on its Enterprise tier (from $4,000 a month). Route 5: Your cloud's own monitoring You already have it, and for a small system it is enough. Service Logs Metrics Traces Amazon CloudWatch (US East) $0.50 per GB ingested, $0.03 per GB a month stored Custom metrics: $0.30 each for the first 10,000, $0.10 for the next 240,000. OpenTelemetry metrics: $0.50 per GB ingested Accepts OpenTelemetry data on its OTLP endpoints Google Cloud Observability $0.50 per GiB, first 50 GiB per project free, 30 days of storage included Managed Service for Prometheus: $0.06 per million samples $0.20 per million spans, first 2.5 million free The strength: no agent contract, no new vendor, access control you already manage. The weakness: it stops at the edge of that cloud, and the classic per-metric price in CloudWatch punishes high cardinality harder than Datadog does. Metrics sent over OTLP are billed per GB instead. A good use of this route is the mix: cloud monitoring for the managed services, an open source stack for your own applications. 500 GB of logs and 20,000 metrics, priced on each tool Price lists are hard to compare because every unit is different. So here is 1 workload on each of them. Every tool bills a different unit, so price your own volume on each. First, 500 GB of logs in a month (300 million events), all of it searchable: Calculation Per month Retention at that price Datadog 500 GB x $0.10 + 300 million events x $1.70 per million $560 15 days Grafana Cloud Pro (500 - 50 included) x $0.55 $247.50 30 days 500 x $0.30 $150 500 x $0.40 $200 465.7 GiB x $0.20 $93.13, plus retention per GiB-day and a charge per GiB scanned You choose, 1 day to 10 years Amazon CloudWatch 500 x $0.50 $250, plus $0.03 per GB a month stored and a charge per GB scanned by queries You choose Google Cloud Logging (465.7 GiB - 50 free) x $0.50 $207.83 Dynatrace and Google bill per GiB, and 500 GB is 465.7 GiB. New Relic's free 100 GB a month covers all your data together, so I left it out of the row. The Grafana Cloud prices are its "starts at" figures, without the $19 platform fee. The Datadog row drops to $203 if exclusion filters leave 30% of the events indexed (Route 1). Compare the cleaned-up number, or the comparison flatters the alternative. Second, 20,000 metric series, each reporting once a minute. That is 864 million samples in a 30 day month: Datadog, as custom metrics on 50 Pro hosts (20,000 - 5,000 included) / 100 x $5 $750 (20,000 - 10,000 included) / 1,000 x $6.50 $65 864 million samples x $0.10 per million $86.40 Google Managed Service for Prometheus 864 million samples x $0.06 per million $51.84 Amazon CloudWatch, classic custom metrics 10,000 x $0.30 + 10,000 x $0.10 $4,000 Amazon CloudWatch, OpenTelemetry metrics 864 million data points x 300 to 600 bytes = 259 to 518 GB, x $0.50 $130 to $259 Read this table with one warning. On Datadog, the metrics that come from its integrations are covered by the host price. Only your custom metrics are counted. On a tool priced per series or per sample, EVERY series counts: the ones from your Kubernetes nodes, your pods and your databases too. So count your real series before you celebrate. Run this in any Prometheus that scrapes your cluster: count({__name__=~".+"}) The number it returns is your active series count. Then check your scrape interval. The table assumes 1 sample a minute. At a 15 second interval you send 4 times the samples: the per-sample rows are 4 times larger, and Grafana Cloud bills 4 data points a minute as 4 series. On Grafana Cloud, add the Kubernetes Monitoring hours from Route 3 if you want that app. The pattern across both tables: the open source based tools are cheaper per unit, and they count more units. The switch costs more than the tool A new observability tool is a migration project. These are the things that move: What you have in Datadog What it becomes Work The Datadog Agent and its integrations The OpenTelemetry Collector, or Prometheus exporters Per integration Tracing libraries (dd-trace) in every service OpenTelemetry SDKs Per service: the largest item Custom metrics sent with DogStatsD The same calls, received by a Collector or by a store that accepts the format Small, with a test first: the Collector's statsd receiver is beta Dashboards Rebuilt, or translated where a tool exists Per dashboard Monitors Alert rules in the new tool Per monitor, with the thresholds checked again Log pipelines, parsing rules and archives Processors in the Collector, plus the new tool's own pipeline Per pipeline Links in runbooks, habits during incidents New links, a practice session Per team Do not rebuild every dashboard. Use the move to delete. List the dashboards opened in the last 90 days and the monitors that paged someone. Migrate those. The rest was decoration. If your monitors are a pile of noise today, moving them moves the noise. Fix that list first: how to handle alert fatigue. Move to OpenTelemetry before you pick OpenTelemetry is the open standard for producing and shipping telemetry. It became a Graduated project of the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) in May 2026, and every tool on this page accepts it (VictoriaMetrics for metrics only). Datadog accepts it too. That is the useful part. You can change how telemetry leaves your services while Datadog stays your tool: Run the OpenTelemetry Collector in the cluster Point your services at the Collector Export from the Collector to Datadog's OTLP intake Add a second exporter when you want to try another tool The relevant part of the Collector config then looks like this (trimmed from the setup Datadog documents, with a second destination added): exporters: otlp_http/datadog: endpoint: https://otlp.${env:DD_SITE} headers: dd-api-key: ${env:DD_API_KEY} otlp_http/candidate: endpoint: ${env:CANDIDATE_OTLP_ENDPOINT} authorization: ${env:CANDIDATE_OTLP_TOKEN} service: pipelines: traces: receivers: [otlp] exporters: [otlp_http/datadog, otlp_http/candidate] logs: The same spans and logs now reach both tools. Your services did not change. One Collector, two destinations. Your services did not change. The header name for the second tool depends on the vendor. The exporter is named otlp_http since Collector v0.144.0 (older versions call it otlphttp), and Datadog's page asks for Collector Contrib v0.154.0 or later. Datadog's full example adds processors, a metrics pipeline with a delta conversion, and a connector that produces the APM metrics. Start from their page and add the second exporter. 3 caveats, all from the docs: Metrics you send over OTLP count as Datadog custom metrics unless they come from a receiver Datadog supports. Move traces and logs first, and check the custom metrics line before you move metrics Some Datadog features expect Datadog's own libraries. Check Datadog's OpenTelemetry compatibility table for the ones you use If you cannot touch the services yet, the Collector has a Datadog receiver that accepts traffic from the Datadog Agent and tracing libraries. It is marked alpha, so treat it as a bridge for the migration Lock-in = instrumentation in one vendor's format. OpenTelemetry removes it without removing the vendor. Run both tools side by side, then cut over The plan I would follow, in order: Clean up: apply Route 1, delete dead dashboards and monitors, write down the monthly volume per signal Shortlist 2 tools: price your real volume on each, in their units Dual-ship 1 service: add the second exporter for one team's services Rebuild the top 10: the 10 dashboards and the paging monitors for that team, in the new tool Run both for at least 2 weeks: include an on-call rotation and one real incident or a game day Decide with the on-call engineers: could they find the cause as fast as before? Roll out by team: then remove the Datadog exporter, the Agent and the contract lines, in that order Both tools run side by side from step 3 until the roll-out. During the parallel run you pay twice for the services you dual-ship. Keep that set small and the period short. Time the cut-over to your renewal date. A migration that ends a month after the renewal costs you a year of commitment. Keep your SLO dashboards and their alerts for last, and move them only after the new numbers match the old ones. Mistakes that make a migration expensive Comparing list prices in different units: hosts against GB against series. Price your own volume Comparing against the uncleaned Datadog bill: the alternative wins a contest it should have had to fight Forgetting the series you never paid for: integration metrics are included in a Datadog host and billed on a per-series tool Self-hosting with nobody assigned: the stack works until the first upgrade Migrating everything: every dashboard moved, a few of them opened Cutting over without a parallel run: you find the missing alert during the incident it was for Switching tool and instrumentation in the same month: change the instrumentation first, while the old tool still shows you what broke The checklist Always: Write down the products you use and the reason you want to leave Cut the Datadog bill before you compare Count your active series, your log GB and your trace GB for a month Price that volume on 2 tools, with retention and users included Ask every vendor for the minimum commitment and the overage price Send telemetry through an OpenTelemetry Collector before you choose Run both tools for at least 2 weeks Let the people on call make the final call Name the owner of the new stack, especially when it is self-hosted FAQ Who is Datadog's biggest competitor? Among commercial platforms, Dynatrace and New Relic sell the closest thing: one product for metrics, traces and logs. Among open source options, the Grafana stack is the one most teams compare it with. Is there a free alternative to Datadog? Yes, at small scale. Grafana Cloud's free plan includes 10,000 metric series and 50 GB each of logs and traces, New Relic includes 100 GB a month and 1 full platform user, and Honeycomb includes 20 million events a month. Datadog has a free plan too: up to 5 hosts with 1 day of metric retention. Is there an open source Datadog alternative? Yes. The common ones are the Grafana stack (Prometheus, Loki, Tempo, Grafana) and SigNoz. Both can be self-hosted, and both are sold as a managed service by the company behind them. Is Grafana better than Datadog? Grafana is cheaper per unit and open source, and Datadog needs less setup. I would choose Grafana Cloud when cost and lock-in are the problem, and stay on Datadog when the team is small and the bill is under control. Why is Datadog so expensive? Because the bill follows usage that nobody approves: indexed log events, custom metric tag combinations, containers and APM hosts. The $15 host price is a small part of it. My pricing breakdown shows a 50 host bill where it is 17%. Can I use OpenTelemetry with Datadog? Yes. Datadog accepts OTLP through the Datadog Agent, through an OpenTelemetry Collector and on direct intake endpoints. Start with traces and logs: OTLP metrics can count as custom metrics on the Datadog bill. How long does it take to move off Datadog? The parallel run sets the minimum: 2 weeks. The rest depends on how many services still use Datadog's tracing libraries and how many dashboards and monitors you decide to keep. A recap If you take away 1 thing, let it be this: Fix the bill first, standardize on OpenTelemetry second, and choose the tool third. In that order, the choice is small and you can change it again. You don't need a consultant for this. The steps are above, and the Datadog pricing breakdown has the filters and the numbers for the first one. (Yes, I sell DevOps engineers.) If you would rather have a senior engineer go over the bill and the options with you, book a free 30-minute consultation.

articles.title: How to get a company's open jobs straight from Greenhouse, Lever or Ashby
articles.description: You have a list of companies and want their open roles in one table, with no browser and no HTML parsing. Most careers pages built on Greenhouse, Lever or Ashby are rendered from a public JSON endpoint that anyone can call, and the three are similar enough to merge into one shape. The three endpoints The board token is the last part of the careers URL: job-boards.greenhouse.io/, jobs.lever.co/, jobs.ashbyhq.com/. An unknown token returns 404 on all three. Greenhouse: GET https://boards-api.greenhouse.io/v1/boards//jobs. One request returns the whole board (674 jobs for the board I tried, in about a second). You get id, title, location.name, first_published, updated_at and absolute_url. Descriptions need ?content=true, which made that same response about 10 MB. Pay is not in the list; /jobs/?pay_transparency=true adds pay_input_ranges when the company publishes one, one request per job. Lever: GET https://api.lever.co/v0/postings/?mode=json. Descriptions are included, createdAt is epoch milliseconds, and the location sits in categories.location. Large boards are slow: an 85-posting board took about 10 seconds today. Lever also pages with skip and limit, and has an EU host, api.eu.lever.co. Ashby: GET https://api.ashbyhq.com/posting-api/job-board/. One request for the board. Add ?includeCompensation=true for pay ranges where published, which made one board's response about 3 MB. Normalise them import json, urllib.request from datetime import datetime, timezone def get(url): req = urllib.request. Request(url, headers={"User-Agent": "careers-feed-example/1.0 (personal script)"}) with urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=60) as r: return json.load(r) def greenhouse(board): for j in get(f"https://boards-api.greenhouse.io/v1/boards/{board}/jobs")["jobs"]: yield dict(ats="greenhouse", id=str(j["id"]), title=j["title"].strip(), location=j["location"]["name"], posted=j["first_published"], url=j["absolute_url"]) def lever(site): for j in get(f"https://api.lever.co/v0/postings/{site}?mode=json"): yield dict(ats="lever", id=j["id"], title=j["text"].strip(), location=j["categories"].get("location"), posted=datetime.fromtimestamp(j["createdAt"] / 1000, timezone.utc).isoformat(), url=j["hostedUrl"]) def ashby(board): for j in get(f"https://api.ashbyhq.com/posting-api/job-board/{board}")["jobs"]: yield dict(ats="ashby", id=j["id"], title=j["title"].strip(), location=j["location"], posted=j["publishedAt"], url=j["jobUrl"]) Output (one run): greenhouse 674 jobs; first: 3P Revenue Accounting & Reporting | San Francisco, CA | Seattle, WA | 2026-10-19T11:17:24-04:00 lever 10 jobs; first: Customer Success Manager | Atlanta, Georgia | 2026-08-31T18:12:19.703000+00:00 ashby 176 jobs; first: Security Engineer, Cloud | New York, NY (HQ) | 2026-04-07T17:12:35.753+00:00 The .strip() on titles is there because one Ashby title came back with a leading space. The Lever board here is Lever's own demo board, leverdemo, which is why it has only 10 jobs. Spot new and removed postings Postings have stable ids, so a daily diff is a set comparison. Save the previous ids, print what is new, and print what disappeared. Save the first script as ats.py; this one imports from it. import json from ats import greenhouse, lever jobs = {f'{j["ats"]}:{j["id"]}': j for j in [*greenhouse("anthropic"), *lever("leverdemo")]} try: old = json.load(open("jobs_last.json")) except FileNotFoundError: old = None if old is not None: for key in jobs.keys() - old.keys(): print("NEW ", jobs[key]["title"], "|", jobs[key]["url"]) for key in old.keys() - jobs.keys(): print("REMOVED", old[key]["title"], "|", old[key]["url"]) print(len(jobs), "open jobs saved") To test it I ran it once, deleted one entry from jobs_last.json, added a fake one, and ran it again: NEW 3P Revenue Accounting & Reporting | https://job-boards.greenhouse.io/anthropic/jobs/5456619008 REMOVED Ghost role | https://example.com/1 684 open jobs saved A reposted job usually gets a new id, so it shows up as one removal and one new posting. If that matters, match on title and location as well. Limits and gotchas Each API exposes different fields. Lever has no company name, no updated date and no requisition id. Ashby has no company name or updated date. Greenhouse has no employment type or pay in the list. Ashby's isRemote is unreliable. It is set on many hybrid jobs, so read workplaceType instead. Placeholders pass through. Some Greenhouse boards fill requisition_id with a literal like "See Opening ID" on every job. Greenhouse descriptions are HTML-escaped, so decode them before converting to text. Board names are first-come slugs. The same name on two systems can be two different companies, and companies leave stale boards behind when they switch. Check the job URL before trusting a match. Coverage is partial. Workday, iCIMS, Taleo and custom careers sites have no public feed like this. Be gentle. One request per board per day is enough. These endpoints exist so careers pages and aggregators can read them; keep to that use, collect job data only, and leave applicant or recruiter details alone. If you don't want to maintain this yourself Disclosure: I'm the developer of an Apify Actor, ATS Jobs Scraper, published under Cedarfetch Labs. It covers seven systems instead of three (it adds SmartRecruiters, Workable, Recruitee and Personio), returns one schema for all of them, and tracks changes between scheduled runs, labelling each job new, updated, unchanged or removed. A job is only marked removed after a complete, error-free read of the board. It is pay per event: $0.0015 per job row (removed rows included) plus $0.00005 per run start, as shown on the listing on 2026-11-11. Check the Pricing tab for current figures. Listing: https://apify.com/cedarfetch/ats-jobs-scraper Runnable Python, Node.js and cURL examples for the Actor: https://github.com/cedarfetch/ats-jobs-scraper-examples Not affiliated with Greenhouse, Lever or Ashby.

articles.title: How to make an AI drama with the same cast in every episode
articles.description: Disclosure: an AI assistant (Claude) drafted this story for the RefVid team. Every image below is a still from our own AI-generated clips or a drawn character sheet, not a photograph of a real person. Most AI video tools start each clip from one picture or from words alone, so a face drifts a little every time. That is fine for one clip and fatal for a drama, where viewers have to recognise the lead in episode ten. This is the method we use to keep one cast across episodes, with the real clips and prompts behind it. Save each character once Give every character a small set of reference photos instead of a single portrait. One clear portrait is enough to start, and three to five hold a face better: straight on, three-quarter from each side, and one waist-up in the costume they wear all season. Invented characters work the same way, as a portrait from an image tool or a drawn character sheet. Mia and Leo, two invented actors: one of the eight reference photos saved once and reused in every scene. Every scene you generate then starts from those saved photos, so the model sees the same faces from several angles in each new clip. Several characters can share one shot, each tied to their own photos, so a couple, a rival and a boss keep their faces apart. The cast stays in your account, and the next episode starts from the same saved characters instead of new uploads. Shoot one scene at a time Write the episode as four to eight scenes of 10 to 15 seconds, with the spoken lines in quotes. Here is a scene prompt that works, the one behind the café clip below: Rainy evening in a quiet café: Mia and Leo sit across a small table, untouched coffee between them. Wide shot, moody window light. Close-up of Mia, eyes steady, saying quietly: ‘You knew all along, didn’t you?’ Close-up of Leo, looking down, then up, and answering: ‘I was going to tell you tonight.’ The result is a 10-second vertical clip with spoken dialogue and room sound, made on Kling 3.0 Omni from the same saved photos. A still from the café scene: Mia and Leo, 10 seconds, vertical, with dialogue. A cast that survives a whole series The same method scales past one scene. Our own cartoon series, GuaPi, has four episodes, and each of its four characters was drawn once and saved once. Every episode draws on those same character sheets, so Henry, Alice, GuaPi the goose and Xiaobai look the same in episode four as in episode one. Henry, from the GuaPi character sheets. GuaPi the goose, saved once and used in all four episodes. A still from GuaPi Episode 3: 36 seconds on Kling 4, drawn from the same character sheets. For a beat with no dialogue, a plain action line is enough. From Episode 1: The little fan sparks and bursts with a pop: a thick cloud of black smoke explodes out of it, the blades jam and stop, the umbrella jolts; Henry’s grin turns into wide-eyed panic. Keep the drawn style. End every episode on an open action, such as a phone lighting up or a door opening, and start the next one from it. Checks before you post an episode Compare the costumes with last time, spell the names the same way in every caption, and check the faces side by side with episode one. Switch on the AI label wherever the platform asks for it. Get consent from every real person in the cast, and never use the face of someone who has not agreed. Keep the scene prompts and the saved cast together, so a scene that needs a redo can be made again with the same characters. The whole method, with both prompts, the step-by-step table and the answers to the usual questions, is on one page: the RefVid AI drama generator page. Louis Chi

articles.title: CVE-2026-129433: Dokploy 9.9 — The Access Control Is the Member List
articles.description: CVE-2026-129433 is a CVSS 9.9 authenticated RCE in Dokploy, the self-hosted Docker deployment platform. Vector: AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:H The PR:L requires an account. The S:C scope change crosses from the web app to the Docker host. The result is root on the host — every container, every env var, every secret the team deployed. Why PR:L is thin on a team platform: Dokploy's access model is an org member list. The precondition is the product's normal usage. What to do: Upgrade to the fixed release (confirm versions from the Dokploy advisory) Audit the org member list — remove stale accounts, shared logins; enable MFA Treat the Docker host as tier zero — segment it, monitor it If exposed on a vulnerable version: rotate all secrets reachable from the host The access control for this CVE is the member list. The audit is part of the fix the patch doesn't perform. Full write-up: https://threataft.com/articles/cve-2026-129433-dokploy-authenticated-rce-docker

articles.title: Claude Code OpenTelemetry: Drop user.email, Sum the Deltas
articles.description: If you want to record your own or your team's Claude Code telemetry (token, cost and session usage), its OpenTelemetry export (sent over OTLP, the open standard protocol for logs and metrics) will do it, and it writes your signed-in account email onto log records and metric points whenever the email is available. I set up a local OpenTelemetry Collector (a small service that receives and forwards that data) that deletes that field and writes plain JSON lines. Summing the points in those files gives Claude Code token usage and cost totals that add up, as long as no points go missing. When you finish, you have a collector listening only on localhost that keeps session, token and cost records on local disk without the email. One counting rule matters: each metric point (one numeric reading per export) is a delta (only the change since the previous export), so the total is the sum of all points. Reading the last point gives you the wrong number. The OpenTelemetry export carries user.email Turning the export on takes a handful of environment variables. What comes with them is the problem. Claude Code's monitoring docs mark user.email as "Always included when available." They list switches for some other attributes, such as the session ID, account UUID and version. None of the switches covers the email. The fix is a drop processor (the attributes processor with action: delete): one collector rule that deletes a named field before anything is written. In an early trial without the rule, the token usage points carried user.email among 11 attribute keys. With the rule in place, a pre-install trial of two short headless Claude Code sessions against a scratch collector showed the email on 0 of 150 log records and 0 of 14 metric points. The account UUID and organization ID stayed. They are opaque IDs rather than an address, though each is still stable per account, and they are what lets you split usage per account. OpenTelemetry Collector config for Claude Code Claude Code gets the environment block below. The endpoint is the loopback HTTP receiver. The host name and namespace are placeholders. I left OTEL_LOG_USER_PROMPTS and OTEL_LOG_TOOL_DETAILS unset. The docs say prompt content is logged only when the first one is set. Setting or removing any of these keys affects new sessions only. The collector side, with both pipelines: receivers: otlp: protocols: http: endpoint: 127.0.0.1:14318 processors: attributes/drop-email: actions: - key: user.email action: delete exporters: file/metrics: path: /data/metrics.jsonl format: json flush_interval: 5s rotation: {max_megabytes: 100, max_days: 0, max_backups: 0} file/logs: path: /data/logs.jsonl service: pipelines: metrics: receivers: [otlp] processors: [attributes/drop-email] # memory_limiter and batch omitted here exporters: [file/metrics] logs: processors: [attributes/drop-email] exporters: [file/logs] The real config also has a gRPC receiver, a health check, memory_limiter and batch, and a second exporter on each pipeline that feeds a local SigNoz backend. All listeners bind 127.0.0.1. Processors run before exporters, so the email is gone before any exporter sees the record. max_days: 0 turns off age-based removal, and max_backups: 0 keeps every rotated file. There is no compression key, so the output is plain JSON lines. Why not the obvious approach? Three moves look reasonable at first. I rejected all three: one after testing it, one after it had already put a wrong rule in the notes. Compress the file. The file exporter has a zstd mode, and it is the first thing you reach for with a log file. In the first trial, telemetry from headless Claude Code sessions landed in a zstd file that neither zstdcat nor jq could read. I reproduced it with one probe record posted to the HTTP receiver. The file came back with a binary prefix and was not JSON: $ od -A d -t x1 -N 8 logs.jsonl 0000000 00 00 00 8a 28 b5 2f fd $ jq -c . logs.jsonl # exit status 5 zstdcat could not decode it either; it printed the raw length-prefixed bytes. Stripping the 4-byte big-endian length and decoding the first frame (138 bytes) recovered JSON containing the probe. The data survived, but the standard tools could not read the file as delivered. I removed compression. The plan is for Borg (the nightly backup tool) to compress the files at backup time instead. The first archive containing them was still pending, so that part is not yet proven. Allowlist the attributes. An allowlist keeps the fields you name and drops everything else. It is the safer default for fields you have not read yet, and it could keep the account UUID and organization ID just as well. I chose the single delete rule anyway, because it is one line and leaves every other field as Claude Code sent it. That is a trade-off, not a win. A delete rule only removes the key it names. A future field that carries an address passes through until someone adds a rule for it, which is why the first check under "Use this" has to be repeated. Read the last point. The metrics are monotonic Sums with delta temporality (aggregationTemporality 1, which is DELTA). Each point is the increment since the previous export. The last point is one interval, not the total. An earlier README note in this build said to take the last cumulative point, and that note was the actual error. One review also argued the metrics were histograms. The trial receipt (a machine-written record that a step really ran) shows they are Sums, so that claim was wrong. Summing delta points for token and cost totals The trial showed four Claude Code metrics (claude_code.session.count, claude_code.cost.usage, claude_code.token.usage and claude_code.active_time.total). These are two of them from one headless session, condensed from the exporter output (in the raw file the field is aggregationTemporality): The window total is the sum of every point in it. Each point is only an increment, so a skipped point undercounts. The live install below lost one session's request event during an outage; metric-point loss was not measured. For a per-account split, group the sums by user.account_uuid. The same numbers also appear on the claude_code.api_request log events, which carry input_tokens, output_tokens and cost_usd. What the reviews caught The first version had real defects. OpenCodeReview (14 findings) and two MiniMax reviews found that it stored the account email. They also found that the installer had no rollback, that a config change on a bind mount never recreated the container, and that claims ran ahead of the evidence. The installer now validates the config first, recreates the container with --force-recreate, and restores the previous copy if the new one does not come up healthy. Its test has 31 cases, 24 of them planted faults. Not every finding was right. Claude Opus 5.5, the build session, accepted the valid findings and refuted two with evidence: the histogram claim, and a claim that an evidence rebinding was missing (it was in the diff). The second MiniMax review, the adversarial one, made me narrow the wording. The 100 MB file rotation is configured. It is not yet exercised. Claude Fable 5.1 ran the headless trial sessions that generated the telemetry, including the first trial that exposed the zstd framing. What the live install showed On the live install, the collector came up with zero restarts and listened on loopback only. No prompt or tool-detail logging keys were set in the settings environment. A session with only the settings change exited 0. API request events went from 0 to 1. A session with the collector stopped exited 0 in 11 seconds. When the collector came back, it was healthy. After a Docker restart, the next session took the events from 1 to 2. The outage session's event never arrived. Claude Code did not hold it for the collector to receive later. Across 140 log records and 14 metric points in the live files, none carried user.email. The email domain appeared 0 times. Four records carried prompt or response attributes. Each held the literal value . What the receipts do not show Prompt and response content in general. The redaction count covers four records from test sessions, not every event type Claude Code can emit. How much an outage loses. The event count shows one session's event went missing. It does not measure metric points lost, or what happens with a longer outage. Backups. The install is marked manually verified, not fully verified, because its sessions were test runs. The first backup archive containing the data directory was still pending. Rotation. Configured, not exercised. A SigNoz outage. That exporter is configured to retry for 60 seconds and then drop. Whether a SigNoz outage affects the file outputs was not tested. Also shipped Set cleanupPeriodDays to 3650, so the 1,581 local session transcripts on disk (2.6 GB) are no longer subject to Claude Code's default cleanup. Added the second exporter to a loopback SigNoz stack, whose first live check landed 71 log rows and 4 token-usage samples with user.email on 0 rows. FAQ Can I keep my email out of Claude Code OpenTelemetry data? None of the documented switches covers user.email, so the fix is a drop processor in a local OpenTelemetry Collector that deletes the field before anything is written. In the pre-install trial the email appeared on 0 of 150 log records and 0 of 14 metric points after the rule, while the account UUID and organization ID stayed. A delete rule only removes the key it names, so a future field that carries an address passes through until a rule is added for it. Check your own output by running one session and grepping the files for your email domain. Are Claude Code OpenTelemetry metrics delta or cumulative? The token and cost metrics are delta. They are monotonic Sums with aggregationTemporality 1, which is DELTA, so each point is the increment since the previous export and the last point covers only one interval. The window total is the sum of every point. A skipped point undercounts, and in the live install a session run while the collector was down never delivered its event. How do I total Claude Code tokens and cost from OpenTelemetry? Sum every delta point of claude_code.token.usage or claude_code.cost.usage in the time window. For a per-account split, group those sums by user.account_uuid. The same figures also appear on claude_code.api_request log events as input_tokens, output_tokens and cost_usd. Do not read the last point, since it covers one export interval only. Use this Check the drop before you trust it, and again after each Claude Code upgrade, since a delete rule misses any new field. Bind the receivers to 127.0.0.1, run one session, then grep -c your email domain across the output files. The trial found zero. Field names are listed in the monitoring docs at https://code.claude.com/docs/en/monitoring-usage. Write plain JSON lines (format: json, no exporter compression), then check them with jq -c . logs.jsonl. That is the check the zstd file failed. Total tokens and cost by summing every delta point in the window, and group by user.account_uuid for a per-account split. Do not read the last point, and keep the collector up, because a session run while it was down never delivered its request event.

articles.title: Dynatrace OTel Collector: migrating from Contrib safely
articles.description: Your Collector runs the Contrib image, and someone has asked you to move to the Dynatrace OTel Collector. Before you touch a line of configuration, one question matters: what actually changes? This article skips the tour of Contrib, which our Contrib components guide already covers. It looks only at the gap between the two builds and at the migration path. What I read: the introduction and deployment pages of the Dynatrace documentation, then the README of the GitHub repository, on 9 November 2026. Version numbers are those shown on those pages that day. I did not run the binary, so anything about runtime behaviour is flagged as unverified. Dynatrace OTel Collector: a curated subset, not a fork The documentation is explicit. The distribution keeps the standard configuration model and component semantics, with no proprietary abstractions and no hidden defaults. In practice, a YAML file written for Contrib stays readable as it is. The difference lies in what is compiled into the binary. Contrib ships a very large number of third-party receivers, processors and exporters. Dynatrace advises against it in production and keeps it for testing, because it uses more storage and memory than a targeted build. The Dynatrace distribution contains only components the vendor says it has verified for common use cases. The full list lives in the GitHub repository, not in the documentation. What the distribution removes: read the list before you switch This is where migrations go wrong. A component missing from the binary stops the Collector from starting, because it rejects a configuration that names an unknown component. Here is what I found in the README’s Components section. Receivers: otlp, filelog, hostmetrics, prometheus, statsd, syslog, fluentforward, jaeger, zipkin, kafka, kafka_metrics and four Kubernetes receivers (k8sobjects, k8scluster, kubelet_stats, k8sevents). Journald and netflow are alpha. Processors: batch, memory_limiter, attributes, resource, resource_detection, transform, k8sattributes, cumulativetodelta, metricstarttime, probabilistic_sampler, tail_sampling and groupbytrace, plus filter, redaction and genainormalizer in alpha. Exporters: otlp, otlphttp, debug and kafka, plus load_balancing in alpha. Extensions and connectors: bearertokenauth, oidcauth, healthcheck, zpages, k8sleaderelector and filestorage; forward and, in alpha, spanmetrics. I could not find a Prometheus Remote Write exporter, a file exporter, a SQL receiver or a Docker receiver in that list. If your pipelines rely on one of them, you need another route. That absence comes from my reading of the README. I did not compile the binary to confirm it. What you get in return The distribution adds no hidden feature. It adds guarantees around the binary. Bounded vendor support: x86-64 and ARM64 builds are covered by Dynatrace Support. Each minor version is supported for three months, with fixes shipped as a patch on the latest supported minor or in the next minor. Independent security patches: Dynatrace says it receives them without waiting for upstream Collector releases. Signed images: they are signed with cosign from version 0.49.0 and published on GHCR, Amazon ECR Public and Docker Hub. Limited support for everything else: for Contrib, Dynatrace only covers the components and versions present in its own distribution. GitHub issues are handled on a best-effort basis, with no contract or SLA. So the trade is fewer components for a supported perimeter. For an SRE team, it also means less surface to patch, and therefore less toil with every CVE. Migrating from Contrib in five steps This is the route I would follow. It starts from your real configuration, not from the documentation. List the components you use. With yq (version 4), print what your pipelines name, then the extensions: yq '.service.pipelines[] | .receivers[], .processors[], .exporters[]' config.yaml \ | sed 's#/.*##' | sort -u yq '.service.extensions[]' config.yaml | sed 's#/.*##' | sort -u Compare with the repository list. Each missing component falls into one of three cases: drop it, replace it, or keep it in a second Contrib or OCB Collector upstream. Wire up the Dynatrace exporter. The deployment page gives the example below, reading the endpoint and token from the environment: Change the image or package. The deployment page points to version 0.60.0 (dynatrace/dynatrace-otel-collector:0.60.0 on Docker Hub). Pin an exact version rather than latest. Switch gradually. Move one gateway first, compare, then extend to the agents. One detail to test: the documentation example names the exporter otlp_http, while many Contrib configurations write otlphttp. I do not know whether version 0.60.0 accepts both names. Run the validation before you roll out widely. How to check that it works Validate the file first, then watch the signals. One command covers the first part: ./dynatrace-otel-collector validate --config=config.yaml That subcommand exists in the upstream Collector, but I did not test it on this binary. It catches unknown components before deployment. After that, on the operations side: Temporarily add the debug exporter to watch data go by. Enable the healthcheck extension: the Helm examples in the documentation expose it on port 13133. Compare received and exported volumes before and after, signal by signal. In Dynatrace, confirm that traces arrive, for example using the attributes described in the anatomy of an OpenTelemetry span. Deploying: three routes on Kubernetes The deployment page separates agent mode (a Collector next to the application) from gateway mode (a standalone service, often one per cluster). On Kubernetes, three routes exist: the Dynatrace Operator, from version 1.11.0, which resolves the Collector image by itself (see our Dynatrace Operator guide); the OpenTelemetry Operator, which requires cert-manager (see the OpenTelemetry Operator article); the open-telemetry/opentelemetry-collector Helm chart, with the alternateConfig block that replaces the default configuration. Credentials go in a Kubernetes secret, named dynatrace-otelcol-dt-api-credentials in the examples, holding DT_ENDPOINT and DT_PLATFORM_TOKEN. The examples cap memory at 512 Mi, so adjust it to your load. Outside Kubernetes, the documentation also covers Docker, plain binaries and DEB and RPM packages. Managed or SaaS: what I could not confirm The examples I read use a platform token, which matches a SaaS environment. I did not verify the endpoint and token to use on Dynatrace Managed. For Managed, start from our step-by-step guide to the Collector and Dynatrace and check the ingest address on your own cluster. The exact token scopes are not in the pages I read either. Best practices Version the list of components you use next to the configuration: it becomes a check at every upgrade. Plan one minor upgrade per quarter, since a minor version is supported for three months. Treat alpha components as unstable: the repository says they may change significantly. Keep a second, chained Collector for exotic sources rather than giving up the supported distribution. Never put the token in the file: use an environment variable or a secret. Frequently asked questions Is the Dynatrace OTel Collector compatible with a Contrib configuration? For the format, yes: the documentation states that the configuration model stays standard. For components missing from the binary, no, and they block startup. Check the list before you switch. Can you send data to Dynatrace with Contrib? Yes, the protocol is OTLP either way. The difference is support: for Contrib, it is limited to the components and versions included in the Dynatrace distribution. What if a component is missing? Build a custom Collector with the OpenTelemetry Collector Builder, or chain two Collectors: the custom build for the exotic source, the Dynatrace distribution as the exit towards the platform. Conclusion The Dynatrace OTel Collector does not change how you write a configuration. It changes what the binary accepts and what the vendor agrees to support. List your components, compare them with the repository, then switch one Collector at a time. The payoff is a smaller surface and faster fixes. span.observer is an independent community blog, not affiliated with Dynatrace LLC. Brands mentioned belong to their owners. Tools change quickly: check versions, components and commands in the official documentation and the GitHub repository. Originally published on span.observer. French version: https://span.observer/fr/dynatrace-otel-collector-migrer-contrib/.
